title: A Cell Cannot Name a Molecule

scenes.tts: A mouse has about a thousand odorant-receptor genes. It reads an odour from a pattern across its receptors.
scenes.visual: A mouse nose, with a counter: about 1,000 odorant-receptor genes. Many coloured dots form a pattern.
scenes.narration: A mouse has about a thousand odorant-receptor genes. It reads an odour from a pattern across its receptors.

scenes.tts: It also has dozens of bitter-receptor genes. Yet bitter is one taste. Why the difference?
scenes.visual: A tongue beside the nose: dozens of bitter-receptor shapes funnel into one word, BITTER. Question on screen: Why the difference?
scenes.narration: It also has dozens of bitter-receptor genes. Yet bitter is one taste. Why the difference?

scenes.tts: Start with one receptor cell. Its output is its activity: how strongly it is active.
scenes.visual: A single receptor cell with a meter on top showing its activity level.
scenes.narration: Start with one receptor cell. Its output is its activity: how strongly it is active.

scenes.tts: Two different molecules arrive, each at a concentration that activates it equally.
scenes.visual: Molecule X arrives at low concentration; molecule Y, a different shape, arrives at higher concentration. Labels: invented example.
scenes.narration: Two different molecules arrive, each at a concentration that activates it equally.

scenes.tts: Can this cell tell which molecule it met?
scenes.visual: Both meter readings shown side by side, identical. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Can this cell tell which molecule it met?

scenes.tts: No. A receptor cell reports how strongly it is active, not which molecule activated it.
scenes.visual: The two identical meters merge into one. Text: a cell reports how strongly it is active, not which molecule activated it.
scenes.narration: No. A receptor cell reports how strongly it is active, not which molecule activated it.

scenes.tts: Vision calls this univariance. A cone cannot tell a dim light near its peak from a brighter one far from it.
scenes.visual: A cone cell lit by a dim light near its peak colour, then by a brighter light of a far colour; same response. Label: univariance.
scenes.narration: Vision calls this univariance. A cone cannot tell a dim light near its peak from a brighter one far from it.

scenes.tts: To tell molecules apart when their concentrations vary, a sense needs more than one line. A line is a set of cells whose activity reaches the brain as one channel.
scenes.visual: Definition on screen: line = a set of cells whose activity reaches the brain as one channel.
scenes.narration: To tell molecules apart when their concentrations vary, a sense needs more than one line. A line is a set of cells whose activity reaches the brain as one channel.

scenes.tts: In smell, a line is all the neurons with one receptor, and the glomeruli they converge on.
scenes.visual: Nose epithelium: scattered neurons of one colour, axons converging on two glomeruli in the olfactory bulb. Label: about two per bulb.
scenes.narration: In smell, a line is all the neurons with one receptor, and the glomeruli they converge on.

scenes.tts: In taste, a line is one kind of receptor cell: the sweet cells, the bitter cells, and so on.
scenes.visual: A taste bud with cells coloured by kind: sweet, bitter, umami, sour.
scenes.narration: In taste, a line is one kind of receptor cell: the sweet cells, the bitter cells, and so on.

scenes.tts: A pattern is the relative strength of activity across lines, not just which lines are on.
scenes.visual: A row of meters at different heights. Definition on screen: pattern = relative strength across lines.
scenes.narration: A pattern is the relative strength of activity across lines, not just which lines are on.

scenes.tts: The rule: a sense can tell two stimuli apart only if their patterns across separate lines differ.
scenes.visual: The boxed rule appears on screen, as in the lesson. Two identical bar patterns are marked: no distinction in this model. Two different ones are marked: can differ in principle; test behaviour.
scenes.narration: The rule: a sense can tell two stimuli apart only if their patterns across separate lines differ.

scenes.tts: Smell keeps about a thousand receptor types on separate lines. So an odour is read as a pattern across many lines.
scenes.visual: Split screen, left: the nose, many coloured neurons, each colour converging on its own glomeruli. Label: about 1,000 separate lines.
scenes.narration: Smell keeps about a thousand receptor types on separate lines. So an odour is read as a pattern across many lines.

scenes.tts: Taste pools its receptors into a few kinds of cell. So a taste is read mainly from which kind of cell is active.
scenes.visual: Right panel: a bitter cell studded with many different receptor shapes and one output wire to the nerve.
scenes.narration: Taste pools its receptors into a few kinds of cell. So a taste is read mainly from which kind of cell is active.

scenes.tts: A line whose activity always means one quality, whatever turned it on, is called a labeled line.
scenes.visual: The bitter cell's output wire gains a tag: BITTER. Label: labeled line.
scenes.narration: A line whose activity always means one quality, whatever turned it on, is called a labeled line.

scenes.tts: Keep the scope in view. The rule is about the periphery, mostly in mice, and it ignores spike timing.
scenes.narration: Keep the scope in view. The rule is about the periphery, mostly in mice, and it ignores spike timing.

scenes.tts: Gene count alone does not set the number of lines. What matters is whether receptor identity is kept separate or pooled.
scenes.visual: Final card: Smell keeps receptor lines separate. Taste pools receptors into a few kinds of cell.
scenes.narration: Gene count alone does not set the number of lines. What matters is whether receptor identity is kept separate or pooled.
